source: Ramsey (1926) Truth and Probability
finding: Ramsey derives the probability laws from preferences over bets. Degrees of belief are measured by the odds a person would just take. Breaking the laws makes choices depend on how options are framed.
numbers: Laws derived: degree of belief in p plus in not-p is 1; multiplication law for p and q given p. No experiments.
quote: He could have a book made against him by a cunning better and would then stand to lose in any event.
limits: Dutch book is a one-line remark, not a theorem. Ramsey treats the laws as consistency, not as truth-guidance.
agent_relevance: Founding case for a sum-to-one guardrail: a set of answer-probabilities that does not add to 1 is internally inconsistent, whatever the facts.

source: Ramsey (1926) Truth and Probability (consistency reading)
finding: Ramsey calls the laws of probability 'laws of consistency', an extension of formal logic to partial belief. They do not say which degree of belief is the right one.
numbers: Single passage near the end of section 3.
quote: the laws of probability are laws of consistency, an extension to partial beliefs of formal logic
limits: Consistency says nothing about accuracy: a dogmatic credence set is coherent. Ramsey says this explicitly.
agent_relevance: Coherence is a floor, not a goal. A forced-sum rule can make answers consistent but cannot make them right; keep it with checks (G3) and calibration.

source: Ramsey (1926) Truth and Probability (measurement problems)
finding: Ramsey lists limits of bet-based measurement: love or hatred of excitement, diminishing marginal utility of money, and 'reluctance to bother about trifles'. He says stakes should be small, but then trifles distort.
numbers: Qualitative; no figures.
limits: These are the first stated objections to reading credence off bets; Hajek and Maher later extend them.
agent_relevance: The agent has no wallet. Its 'bets' are only a thought device; treat the argument as a consistency test, not a claim of real loss.

source: de Finetti (1937) La prevision: ses lois logiques, ses sources subjectives; and (1974) Theory of Probability
finding: De Finetti defines coherence as having no bet set that loses in every outcome. Theorem: forecasts on a finite event set are coherent iff they extend to a probability measure. Known here only through secondary text.
numbers: Theorem is finite: finitely many events and bets.
limits: Not opened as a primary text; stated from Andrews and Sarkar (2026) and SEP.
agent_relevance: This theorem is what lets code test any set of answer-probabilities by linear programming, with no ground truth needed.

source: Vineberg (SEP) Dutch Book Arguments (theorem and converse)
finding: Dutch Book Theorem: betting quotients that break the axioms allow bets with sure loss. Converse theorem (Kemeny 1955, Lehman 1955): quotients that obey the axioms allow no sure-loss book. Shimony (1955) gave a related strict-coherence result.
numbers: Converse holds only for a finite number of bets.
limits: Converse fails once other norms (Reflection, countable additivity) are added; bets must be restricted in form and number.
agent_relevance: Normalising to sum to 1 guarantees no sure loss on that partition, but does not guarantee safety on other event sets.

source: Vineberg (SEP) Dutch Book Arguments (objections)
finding: Main objections: the link from credence to accepting bets is loose; sure loss is not clearly irrational (Maher); Hajek's 'Czech book' gives an incoherent agent a sure gain unless bets must be fair-or-favourable; stakes and risk attitudes distort.
numbers: Qualitative.
limits: Hajek shows the cancellation is avoided by assuming agents accept fair or favourable bets.
agent_relevance: Do not argue for the guardrail from money loss. Argue from measured accuracy gains (see LLM lines) and from consistency.

source: Vineberg (SEP) Dutch Book Arguments (depragmatized versions)
finding: Christensen (1996), Howson and Urbach (1993), Hellman (1997) recast the argument: incoherent credences give conflicting evaluations of the same bet, so they are inconsistent. Skyrms reads Ramsey this way. Briggs and Mahtani extend it.
numbers: Qualitative.
limits: Maher (1997) argues the notion of 'fair' cannot do without utility. Mahtani's version is contested for Reflection.
agent_relevance: A consistency-only reading fits an agent with no stakes: incoherence is a defect in the state, not a bet.

source: Vineberg (SEP) Dutch Book Arguments (diachronic and countable)
finding: Diachronic Dutch books (Lewis 1999, from Teller 1973) argue for conditionalization. Van Fraassen (1989): the book needs the agent to commit in advance to the deviant update rule, so it is weaker. Countable additivity needs infinitely many bets, so loss is only theoretical.
numbers: Teller 1973 and Lewis 1999 give the conditionalization book. Countable case needs infinite bet series.
limits: Contested; see D02 subfield 01 (conditionalization) for the update norm.
agent_relevance: Synchronic sum-to-one is the well-supported part. Do not extend the guardrail to update rules from Dutch books alone.

source: Epistemic Utility Arguments for Epistemic Norms (SEP)
finding: Accuracy route to probabilism (Joyce 1998, Leitgeb and Pettigrew 2010): any incoherent credence function is accuracy-dominated by a coherent one, if accuracy is measured by a strictly proper additive score such as Brier. This replaces the bet argument.
numbers: Leitgeb and Pettigrew (2010) as cited by Zhu and Griffiths: for any incoherent set there is a coherent set closer to the true frequencies.
limits: Needs strict propriety and additivity; Levinstein shows world-varying weights break the dominance argument. Oddie's verisimilitude and Mayo-Wilson and Wheeler's numerical-representability objections apply.
agent_relevance: This gives the exact reason the guardrail pays off: projecting to coherence cannot raise Brier error under the usual score. It is a pure-math guarantee, not an empirical one.

source: Zhu and Griffiths (2024/2025) Incoherent Probability Judgments in Large Language Models
finding: Four LLMs (GPT-4, GPT-3.5-turbo-1106, LLaMA-2-70b, LLaMA-2-7b) gave incoherent probabilities on 24 event pairs (12 weather, 12 politics). Deviations from probabilistic identities followed the human pattern: bigger when positive and negative terms are unbalanced.
numbers: 6 judgments per pair (A, B, A and B, A and not-B, B and not-A, A or B); temperature 0 and 1; 5 repeats at T=1. Larger models deviated less; none reached zero.
limits: Single prompt style; figures give values, not tabulated. Fits a Bayesian Sampler better than Probability Theory plus Noise, but the data do not separate the two.
agent_relevance: Separately asked probabilities for related answers will not sum correctly. Ask for the whole partition together or fix by code (G5).

source: Zhu and Griffiths (2024/2025) Incoherent Probability Judgments in LLMs (mean-variance)
finding: Repeated judgments of the same event at T=1 show an inverted-U link between mean and variance, as in humans. The paper explains incoherence as noisy samples shrunk toward a prior (Bayesian Sampler), not as random noise on a coherent belief.
numbers: Model mean is E = (N p + beta)/(N + 2 beta), so identities with an extra positive term are biased by beta/(N+2beta).
limits: Account is by analogy to human models; autoregressive training is proposed as the cause, not tested.
agent_relevance: Incoherence is systematic (shrinkage to 0.5), so averaging samples alone does not remove it. Use a structural fix.

source: Zhu, Yan and Griffiths (2025) Recovering Event Probabilities from LLM Embeddings via Axiomatic Constraints
finding: Gemma-2-9b-instruct judged probabilities for an event and its complement did not sum to 1. Simple normalisation (divide each by the sum) cut incoherence to near zero with accuracy (MSE) roughly unchanged. A VAE with an additivity constraint on embeddings gave coherent probabilities too.
numbers: Incoherence |P + not-P - 1|: 0.13 train and 0.14 test for judged. Pearson r with true probability 0.80 (train) and 0.73 (test). Llama-3.1-8b: judged incoherence 0.24, recovered 0.07, but MSE of recovered not better. Dice-roll events, 480 test events.
limits: Synthetic dice events; open-weight 8-9B models. Normalisation gave small MSE changes (t=-2.54, p=.01 on train; p=.09 on test). Table layout in the PDF is garbled so only prose figures are used.
agent_relevance: Plain normalisation is cheap, keeps accuracy, and beats a learned method on MSE. Supports doing the sum-to-one step in code.

source: Fluri, Paleka and Tramer (2023/2024) Evaluating Superhuman Models with Consistency Checks
finding: Forecasting questions with logical checks show LLM inconsistency. GPT-3.5-turbo violated the negation check (P(A) + P(not A) = 1) in 52.6% of cases above a 0.2 threshold, GPT-4 in 10.9%. Prompting the model to negate first cut GPT-4 to 2.9%.
numbers: 380 base forecasting questions, 1220 variants; negation from 175 Autocast pairs. Paraphrase violations 30.8% (3.5) and 12.5% (4). Bayes rule violations 68.6% (3.5) and 58.8% (4). Negation prompting on GPT-3.5: 52.6% to 37.1%; paraphrase violations rose 30.8% to 41.3%.
limits: Fixing one check can worsen another (paraphrase got worse on GPT-3.5 after negation prompting). Median of multiple runs with chain of thought was used.
agent_relevance: Negation is nearly solved for strong models; Bayes-rule consistency is not. A partition sum check is cheap but conditional-probability checks need more.

source: Paleka, Sudhir, Alvarez, Bhat, Shen, Wang and Tramer (2025) Consistency Checks for Language Model Forecasters
finding: An arbitrage-based consistency metric over 10 logical checks (Negation, Paraphrase, Consequence, AndOr, And, Or, But, Cond, CondCond, ExpEvidence). Consistency correlates with later Brier score, strongest for Cond.
numbers: Correlation with Brier, scraped set: Cond 0.92 (arbitrage), CondCond 0.78, And 0.68, Negation 0.60; aggregate 0.62 (arbitrage) and 0.85 (frequentist). NewsAPI set: Cond 0.71, aggregate 0.49. Some checks are near zero or negative (Or -0.24, Negation -0.36 on NewsAPI).
limits: Few forecasters; part of the link is that better models do both. MMLU error correlation was 0.38 and 0.55 for comparison. Signal is check-dependent.
agent_relevance: Use consistency as a label-free proxy for accuracy only with the right checks; Cond and And carry signal, Negation alone is weak.

source: Paleka et al. (2025) o1-mini consistency table
finding: Even a reasoning model is often inconsistent. o1-mini violated the Negation check beyond threshold in 58% (scraped) and 52% (NewsAPI) of tuples.
numbers: o1-mini arbitrage violation Frac: Negation 58%/52%, Paraphrase 56%/53%, AndOr 65%/57%, But 60%/63%, Cond 41%/66%; aggregate arbitrage 0.06 on both sets.
limits: Threshold-dependent counts; one reasoning model.
agent_relevance: Reasoning mode does not make an agent coherent on its own. A code-side check is still needed (G10).

source: Paleka et al. (2025) ArbitrageForecaster
finding: A wrapper that queries a base forecaster on a check tuple and returns the arbitraged forecast. Recursive depth raised consistency on the checked rule, best for Negation, then Paraphrase, weakest for ExpEvidence.
numbers: Tested on gpt-4o-mini with recursion depth 0 to 4. No reliable gain in ground-truth forecasting accuracy, and no gain on checks other than the ones arbitraged.
limits: Authors call results preliminary and cost high for recursion. Repaired forecast on one check does not carry to another.
agent_relevance: Coherence repair is local: it fixes the checked relation and not accuracy. Do not claim an accuracy gain from it alone.

source: Andrews and Sarkar (2026) Dutch Books for Language Models
finding: Measures incoherence as the largest guaranteed Dutch-book profit per unit stake, by linear program, on stock-return bin events. Equals the sup-norm distance from the forecast to the coherent set. Needs no outcome labels.
numbers: GPT-OSS-120B baseline: mean profit 0.002067 per unit stake (95% CI 0.001471 to 0.002737); at least 0.1% in 48 of 100 stock-days, at least 0.5% in 15, at least 1% in 6. 365,100 elicitations, 15 models, 100 stock-days.
limits: One domain (stock returns, variance-normalised); elicitation arms tested on one model only; model outputs are not tradable, so profit is a distance measure.
agent_relevance: A direct, label-free coherence meter for the agent: can run in code on any answer set.

source: Andrews and Sarkar (2026) across 15 models
finding: Incoherence varies by about a factor of 100 across models, far more than accuracy. Models with lower incoherence also have lower Brier error.
numbers: Arbitrage profit from 0.002067 (GPT-OSS-120B) to 0.1994 (Mistral Small 3.2). Brier range only 0.1966 to 0.2157. Spearman 0.9143. 101 of 105 model pairs differ on profit versus 32 on Brier.
limits: One pass for non-workhorse models; several models have knowledge cutoffs after the sample window (lookahead possible).
agent_relevance: Coherence separates models better than accuracy does, so it is a sensitive, cheap monitor.

source: Andrews and Sarkar (2026) richer logical structure
finding: More logically linked events raise incoherence. Adding joint two-stock events raised profit; longer horizons did the same.
numbers: Joint events added a mean increase of 0.00244 (CI 0.001971 to 0.002961) over two marginal sets, 50 dates.
limits: Number of events and richness of dependence are mixed; an appendix control suggests richer dependence still lowers coherence.
agent_relevance: The more related answers an agent must hold together, the more a code-side check is needed.

source: Andrews and Sarkar (2026) elicitation arms
finding: Asking for the full event panel in one query drove incoherence almost to zero (rounding level). Complement pairs lowered it; relation-poor pairs raised it. Averaging 5 samples helped only a little.
numbers: 95% of answers were identical over 5 passes, so noise is not the main cause. Instructions arm and headline arm raised incoherence significantly.
limits: GPT-OSS-120B and 14-event panel only. Authors do not expect users to ask this way.
agent_relevance: Ask for all exclusive answers in one call, then normalise in code. Matches guardrail G5.

source: Andrews and Sarkar (2026) irrelevant context
finding: Irrelevant remarks in the prompt raised incoherence, up to an order of magnitude. Largest from a stated gut forecast ('around 70%') and from positive emotion.
numbers: Most of 7 arms significant against baseline; others: anxiety, a phone battery number (anchor), coffee, 10% of savings invested.
limits: Some arms may carry real information; effect sizes shown only in figures.
agent_relevance: Keep the elicitation prompt clean (S1 input hygiene); user hints and anchors hurt coherence.

source: Kotawala (2026) Locally Coherent, Globally Incoherent
finding: Specialist LLM calls that are each coherent can give a joint quote that is not. Example: four specialists quoted a partition with total mass 2.50. A hierarchical Boyle-Dykstra projection removes the residual deterministically.
numbers: 1,876 ensemble cliques, 4-LLM mid-tier panel: residual > 0 on 33 to 94% of cliques, +0.115 nats per bet regret on 1,770 resolved bets (CI +0.056 to +0.187). Gain falls to +0.006 when bettors coherentise.
limits: Preprint; many workshop versions; regret figures depend on allocation rule and mid-tier panel. Per-coordinate averaging avoids the failure.
agent_relevance: If we split a question across calls, the combined answers must be normalised in code. Hint to S3: never let parallel attempts each quote one answer alone.

source: Kotawala (2026) mitigations and frontier rerun
finding: Prompt and LLM-side fixes were weak. Retrieval did not help (mean residual 0.260 to 0.283). Partition-aware prompting 0.066; LLM aggregator 0.028 with 7 of 100 regressions. Code projection reached the QP floor with no extra call. Frontier models cut the residual 39% but did not remove it.
numbers: Frontier panel (Claude-Opus-4.7, GPT-5.5, DeepSeek-V3.2, Llama-4-Maverick): residual > 0 on 97.8% of 268 bets; mean 0.118 to 0.072. Coupling-visible elicitation: 0.519 to 0.298 on 20 partitions, 16 of 20 improved.
limits: Prompt-based repairs hurt already-coherent quotes (9 of 10 worsening cases had baseline under 0.05).
agent_relevance: Direct support for G5: do the sum-to-one step in code, not by asking a model judge, and gate it on a measured residual.

source: Betz and Richardson (2023) Probabilistic coherence, logical consistency, and Bayesian learning: neural language models as epistemic agents
finding: T5 'rankers' pretrained from scratch on consistent synthetic text still violate probability rules (multiplication, commutativity) and, depending on model, more than 15% of transitivity constraints. Self-training on auto-generated text gradually made them probabilistically coherent.
numbers: Small T5 models on synthetic corpora; metrics for probabilistic, logical and Bayesian violations. Exact per-model numbers not recorded here.
limits: Synthetic language, small models; 'Rationality Hypothesis' is a claim from this setup only and may not carry to chat models.
agent_relevance: Coherence can be trained in (self-training), but our agent is not trained; this says the fix must be in the scaffold.

source: Mandel, Karvetski and Dhami (2018) Boosting intelligence analysts' judgment accuracy: What works, what fails?
finding: Fifty UK analysts judged probabilities of four exclusive tribes. Judgments summed far over 1. Coherentizing (projecting to sum 1) cut error, and aggregating on top cut more.
numbers: Sum of four exclusive hypotheses: M = 1.54 (CI 1.33 to 1.76) control, M = 1.77 (1.56 to 1.97) with ACH. MAE 0.23 raw to 0.15 coherentized: 35% cut, d = 0.96. Coherentize plus aggregate: 61% cut from 0.23. Chance after coherentizing: MAE 0.21.
limits: One task, 50 novice analysts (mean experience 14 months), human not LLM. Jon Baron's simple normalisation was also tested and worked similarly.
agent_relevance: This is the source of the 35% in G5. Note the effect size depends on a very incoherent starting point (sum 1.5 to 1.8).

source: Mandel et al. (2018) ACH and coherence
finding: Analysis of competing hypotheses did not help. The ACH group was no more accurate, and marginally less coherent, and after coherentizing the ACH effect was null.
numbers: Unpacking effect did not differ between conditions; after coherentizing the tradecraft effect on accuracy was 0.01 (CI -0.04 to 0.07). Coherentizing helped more in the ACH group (d = 1.37 vs 0.69).
limits: Same single task; ACH is covered in other subfields of this run.
agent_relevance: A method that lists more hypotheses can push probabilities over 1; pair any listing step with a forced normalisation.

source: Redelmeier, Koehler, Liberman and Tversky (1995) Probability judgment in medicine: discounting unspecified possibilities
finding: Physicians' probabilities for exclusive outcomes summed above 100% and rose when the residual category was unpacked into named diagnoses. This is the unpacking effect of support theory.
numbers: Four prognoses of one patient averaged 14%, 26%, 55%, 69% = 164% (CI 134% to 194%). Short list residual 50% vs 69% when unpacked (p < 0.005). Gastroenteritis 31% vs 16%. Binary complements: 78% + 21% = 99% (CI 94 to 104%), n = 149 medical students.
limits: Medical vignettes; small samples; explicit vs implicit hypotheses. Binary case is nearly coherent, so the problem grows with the number of alternatives.
agent_relevance: Listing alternatives inflates their total. For an agent with n options, normalising matters more as n grows; keep a catch-all residual option.

source: Tversky and Koehler (1994) Support theory: a nonextensional representation of subjective probability
finding: Support theory gives probability to descriptions, not events: P(A,B) = s(A)/(s(A)+s(B)). Unpacking an implicit hypothesis into parts raises its judged probability, so judged probabilities of exclusive parts can sum above 1. Binary complements add to 1 by construction. Cited via Redelmeier et al. and Mandel et al.
numbers: No numbers recorded from the primary paper in this session.
limits: Primary paper not opened (paywalled). Described from two papers that I did open.
agent_relevance: Explains why separately judged answers over-sum: each gets its own support. Hints that one joint call helps.

source: Hajek (2008) Arguments for or against Probabilism? and Czech book argument (as described by SEP)
finding: Hajek shows that if sure loss shows irrationality, a mirror 'Czech book' shows a sure gain for the incoherent agent, so the argument proves too much unless bets are fair-or-favourable. Taken from SEP, not the primary paper.
numbers: None recorded.
limits: Primary not opened; an accuracy-based reply is the usual alternative.
agent_relevance: Warns against over-selling the Dutch book argument; use accuracy evidence.
